title: Designing In Virtual Reality & Clo Ai With Holly New (Studioofnew)
description:
Learn how to use CLO AI and VR fashion design to optimize digital fashion workflows, bridge immersive 3D technology, and accelerate AI concept creation in this masterclass. Virtual Reality fashion designer and STUDIOOFNEW CEO Holly New shares actionable insights to elevate 3D apparel design.

Core Insights & Solutions in this Video:

Master CLO AI Prompting: Learn how to prompt AI, develop commercial digital fashion concepts, create flat lays, and generate seamless texturing.

Design in Virtual Reality: Discover how to prototype 3D accessories, sketch intuitively using a VR headset, and build rapid prototypes.

Optimize 3D Workflows: Bridge the gap between AI tools, VR software, and CLO 3D apparel design workflows for maximum efficiency.

Whether you are a digital fashion designer looking to master VR tools or an apparel professional aiming to integrate generative AI into your creative pipeline, this complete webinar provides the exact framework to elevate your design systems.


Video Chapters:
0:00 - Introduction to Digital Fashion Workflows and Holly New
4:50 - STUDIOOFNEW Methodology and Generative AI Integration
12:44 - Bringing CLO AI into the 3D Apparel Workflow
24:10 - Connecting CLO and VR Fashion Workflows
31:02 - Designing Trims with a VR Headset and Virtual Reality Sketching
51:00 - Using CLO for Advanced AI Renders and Concepts

markdown_content: ## Overview: Extending CLO with Virtual Reality (VR) and CLO AI This session explains an immersive fashion workflow that combines **CLO AI**, **CLO 3D**, and **VR** to generate concepts, textures, accessories (trims and buttons), and production-ready garments. It also covers how teams can collaborate globally in real time with or without a VR headset. Holly New (CEO of **Studio of New**) introduces herself as the world’s first **VR fashion designer**, recognized by the **BBC** and **CLO** for work bridging **digital fashion**, especially **gaming**, and leaning into **education**. The webinar is hosted in partnership with **CLO** and focuses on extending **CLO** using VR and CLO AI-backed fashion tooling. ### What attendees are expected to learn Across the session, viewers are guided to: - Navigate **CLO AI** to generate concepts, textures, and fashion visuals. - Develop accessory ideas and **prototype accessories in VR**. - Integrate custom elements into **CLO** (e.g., **trims** and **buttons**). - Use immersive workflows that (according to Holly) reduce time and improve standout output. - Combine **VR + CLO + AI** without disrupting existing pipelines. - Achieve similar results even **without owning a VR headset** (e.g., via screen sharing / viewing). ### Studio of New: background and impact claims Holly frames her work as leadership across **AI, XR, and 3D CAD** for fashion and gaming, emphasizing “tech integration when it’s suitable.” She states she won **CLO’s Best Technical Designer Award in 2025**. Studio of New reports: - Working with **20+ clients** over the last **six months**. - Work spanning gaming and tools like **UEFN** and **Copper Candle**, plus fashion and education (including university-level programs). - A reported average reduction in **sampling rounds by ~40%**. - Faster approval cycles because managers can review designs via **immersive 3D in VR**, regardless of location. - Reduced wastage alongside faster pipelines. --- ## Studio of New’s VR-to-CLO workflow (AI → VR → CLO → rendering) This section describes Holly’s “Studio of New method,” a multi-platform pipeline designed to reduce wasted sampling and accelerate iteration while preserving creative intent. Holly’s method coordinates work across three main platforms: 1. **AI (especially CLO AI)** for fashion-specific image-led ideation and concept generation. 2. **VR** for spatial sketching, modeling exploration, and volume/design testing. 3. **CLO (CLO 3D)** for refinement using precision pattern construction, garment simulation, and production-ready outputs. 4. **Rendering** to finalize visuals. She emphasizes that this is not “just a cool idea,” but used in real client projects, with the reported outcomes including fewer physical samples and accelerated concept-to-production timelines. ### Why the sequence matters Holly argues that combining tools at different “levels” prevents creative loss: - **AI + image-led ideation** creates rapid directions. - **VR** helps rebuild and test concepts in 3D space with faster exploration and better texture/volume filtering. - **CLO** refines the work into production-usable garments and accessories. She presents this as a workflow pyramid moving between exploration and execution—so the user gets capability and iteration speed without sacrificing design intent. --- ## AI in creative fashion: adoption, interoperability, sustainability, and job impact This section discusses how AI is being adopted in fashion, why interoperability challenges matter, and how Holly frames AI’s sustainability and employment impact. ### Adoption and interoperability Holly cites a referenced claim: - **85%** of designers/companies are open to or already using AI. - **40%** of those companies report **interoperability** issues as the top problem—software can’t reliably communicate within their pipelines. ### Sustainability and data centers (water usage context) Holly addresses concerns about AI’s environmental impact, particularly claims about water usage in data centers. She notes: - AI is hosted in **data centers**, which use **water** (and also air) for cooling. - A commonly repeated figure (“**200 glasses of water per prompt**”) lacks verified facts, but the core point remains that water is used. - She frames water as effective at reducing heat and potentially extending service lifespan. - She argues the “bigger picture” includes the same data-center infrastructure used by other services like **cloud storage**, **Netflix**, **Prime**, **Google**, **Bing**, and online banking. ### “AI is coming for our jobs” Holly’s stance: AI changes workflows and job content, but does not replace creative judgment and accountability. She compares AI’s impact to prior tech shifts: - Digital art didn’t remove painters. - Photography didn’t remove photographers. - CAD didn’t remove designers. She claims AI mainly replaces **repetitive drafting** and **manual variation**, which can waste time and resources. She also notes: - New roles (e.g., **VR fashion designer**) didn’t exist just a couple years ago, implying future job evolution. ### Integration vs creativity A core theme: the problem isn’t creativity—it’s **integration**. - Holly distinguishes “experimental AI” (e.g., visible image/text generation tools) from “operational AI” (often invisible, such as recommendation systems used for demand forecasting, pricing optimization, and stock allocation). - She emphasizes targeted AI use to avoid wasted cycles and to build better pipelines. --- ## CLO AI Studio: concept images, try-on, flat lays, and the four prompt types This section explains how CLO AI image generation supports fashion outputs and introduces a practical prompting framework: **iterative**, **instruction**, **explorative**, and **chain prompts**. ### Why CLO AI is different for fashion Holly claims that generic garment generation (e.g., mentioning ChatGPT-style image generation) often struggles with **seam placement** because it’s not designed as a fashion output. CLO AI is positioned as better aligned to fashion needs. ### CLO AI Studio entry points In CLO 3D, Holly points to AI tools accessible from the home area, including: - **AI Render Enhancer** - **Texture Generator** - **Graphic Generator** - **Image Generator** Within Image Generator, she highlights options such as: - **Try on** - **Flat lay** - Render/image generation modes (she references “high dream” during the demo) ### Demo: generating an image from a prompt Holly provides an example prompt: - “A **blue dress** with a **skater skirt** and **pretty white bows on the sleeves**” She demonstrates: - Pressing **Generate** - Waiting for multiple minutes as images are created - Selecting a result to **download** or to **use as an input image** for further edits ### Four key prompt types (with how they’re used) Holly describes four prompt categories (not exhaustive, but the ones she expects users to use most): 1. **Iterative prompts** Step-by-step refinement: edit, generate, then adjust again (“work in that way subconsciously”). 2. **Instruction prompts** Directly tell the AI what you want (most straightforward). 3. **Explorative prompts** Use AI for research and idea bouncing (“help me come up with five different ideas,” or explore variations). 4. **Chain prompts** Break down tasks too large for one go (e.g., trend forecasting: patterns → outfits → styles). She notes these can be combined (e.g., instruction into explorative into iterative). ### Try-on and flat lay After generating: - **Try on** combines a selected garment result with an uploaded AI image of a person to simulate wearing it. - Holly cautions that partial body capture can occur (e.g., not showing the full dress), though sometimes the model morphing works more fully. - **Flat lay** produces a 2D flattened garment view (she notes it’s less visually informative than 3D but still useful). --- ## CLO AI textures and graphics: texture prompts, randomization, and image-to-material workflows This section covers how CLO AI generates fabric textures and graphic elements, including using random prompts and image-based reverse prompting. ### Texture Generator: fabric choices and texture parameters Holly describes CLO AI Texture Generator features: - Fabric choices - Style selection - **Pattern size** - Prompting to generate text/pattern outputs A technique she recommends: - **Reverse prompting**: decide how to describe the texture you want based on an image you’re looking at. - Optionally use AI to help describe the image, then feed that description into CLO AI. She demonstrates: - Selecting a texture type (e.g., “**corduroy**”) - Choosing a style (e.g., “**oil painting**”) - Using **random prompts** - Adjusting a numeric parameter (she mentions changing “size to 2” during the demo) - Generating and saving textures for later use ### Texture result usage Generated textures can be used as: - **Graphics** applied to designs, or - Uploaded as **individual fabric pieces** by replacing/modifying materials in the garment workflow. ### Graphic Generator: style, transparency, and image upload Holly also demonstrates Graphic Generator concepts: - Choose graphic styles (she names examples like **embroidery**, **pop art**, **comic art**) - Select whether the graphic is **transparent** or not - Generate based on text prompts or - Generate from an **uploaded image** (use case: logos) She notes she can generate graphics and save them for application in

The webinar is hosted in partnership with **CLO** and focuses on extending **CLO** using VR and CLO AI-backed fashion tooling. ### What attendees are expected to learn Across the session, viewers are guided to: - Navigate **CLO AI** to generate concepts, textures, and fashion visuals. - Develop accessory ideas and **prototype accessories in VR**. - Integrate custom elements into **CLO** (e.g., **trims** and **buttons**). - Use immersive workflows that (according to Holly) reduce time and improve standout output. - Combine **VR + CLO + AI** without disrupting existing pipelines. - Achieve similar results even **without owning a VR headset** (e.g., via screen sharing / viewing). ### Studio of New: background and impact claims Holly frames her work as leadership across **AI, XR, and 3D CAD** for fashion and gaming, emphasizing “tech integration when it’s suitable.” She states she won **CLO’s Best Technical Designer Award in 2025**. Studio of New reports: - Working with **20+ clients** over the last **six months**. - Work spanning gaming and tools like **UEFN** and **Copper Candle**, plus fashion and education (including university-level programs). - A reported average reduction in **sampling rounds by ~40%**. - Faster approval cycles because managers can review designs via **immersive 3D in VR**, regardless of location. - Reduced wastage alongside faster pipelines. --- ## Studio of New’s VR-to-CLO workflow (AI → VR → CLO → rendering) This section describes Holly’s “Studio of New method,” a multi-platform pipeline designed to reduce wasted sampling and accelerate iteration while preserving creative intent. Holly’s method coordinates work across three main platforms: 1. **AI (especially CLO AI)** for fashion-specific image-led ideation and concept generation. 2. **VR** for spatial sketching, modeling exploration, and volume/design testing. 3. **CLO (CLO 3D)** for refinement using precision pattern construction, garment simulation, and production-ready outputs. 4. **Rendering** to finalize visuals. She emphasizes that this is not “just a cool idea,” but used in real client projects, with the reported outcomes including fewer physical samples and accelerated concept-to-production timelines. ### Why the sequence matters Holly argues that combining tools at different “levels” prevents creative loss: - **AI + image-led ideation** creates rapid directions. - **VR** helps rebuild and test concepts in 3D space with faster exploration and better texture/volume filtering. - **CLO** refines the work into production-usable garments and accessories. She presents this as a workflow pyramid moving between exploration and execution—so the user gets capability and iteration speed without sacrificing design intent.

chunks.content: --- ## CLO AI Studio: concept images, try-on, flat lays, and the four prompt types This section explains how CLO AI image generation supports fashion outputs and introduces a practical prompting framework: **iterative**, **instruction**, **explorative**, and **chain prompts**. ### Why CLO AI is different for fashion Holly claims that generic garment generation (e.g., mentioning ChatGPT-style image generation) often struggles with **seam placement** because it’s not designed as a fashion output. CLO AI is positioned as better aligned to fashion needs. ### CLO AI Studio entry points In CLO 3D, Holly points to AI tools accessible from the home area, including: - **AI Render Enhancer** - **Texture Generator** - **Graphic Generator** - **Image Generator** Within Image Generator, she highlights options such as: - **Try on** - **Flat lay** - Render/image generation modes (she references “high dream” during the demo) ### Demo: generating an image from a prompt Holly provides an example prompt: - “A **blue dress** with a **skater skirt** and **pretty white bows on the sleeves**” She demonstrates: - Pressing **Generate** - Waiting for multiple minutes as images are created - Selecting a result to **download** or to **use as an input image** for further edits ### Four key prompt types (with how they’re used) Holly describes four prompt categories (not exhaustive, but the ones she expects users to use most): 1. **Iterative prompts** Step-by-step refinement: edit, generate, then adjust again (“work in that way subconsciously”). 2. **Instruction prompts** Directly tell the AI what you want (most straightforward). 3. **Explorative prompts** Use AI for research and idea bouncing (“help me come up with five different ideas,” or explore variations). 4. **Chain prompts** Break down tasks too large for one go (e.g., trend forecasting: patterns → outfits → styles). She notes these can be combined (e.g., instruction into explorative into iterative). ### Try-on and flat lay After generating: - **Try on** combines a selected garment result with an uploaded AI image of a person to simulate wearing it. - Holly cautions that partial body capture can occur (e.g., not showing the full dress), though sometimes the model morphing works more fully. - **Flat lay** produces a 2D flattened garment view (she notes it’s less visually informative than 3D but still useful). --- ## CLO AI textures and graphics: texture prompts, randomization, and image-to-material workflows This section covers how CLO AI generates fabric textures and graphic elements, including using random prompts and image-based reverse prompting. ### Texture Generator: fabric choices and texture parameters Holly describes CLO AI Texture Generator features: - Fabric choices - Style selection - **Pattern size** - Prompting to generate text/pattern outputs A technique she recommends: - **Reverse prompting**: decide how to describe the texture you want based on an image you’re looking at. - Optionally use AI to help describe the image, then feed that description into CLO AI.
